title: Fight like a warrior
hookLine: a first martial-arts class starts with the stance, not the punch; Shantideva's warrior wins by not bowing
tomorrow: you look straight at an urge. where does it go?

cards: A first martial-arts class often has very little punching in it. It's feet. Where they go, how wide, how the knees bend, where the weight sits.
A teacher walks the line and gives each student a gentle shove on the shoulder. The ones who are standing well don't fall over. They don't push back, either.
They just stay. That's the answer to yesterday's question, and it's Shantideva's answer too. A warrior against craving starts with how they stand.

teach.b: Shantideva looks around at people who bear hardship for much smaller prizes. Farmers and fishermen putting up with heat and cold to make a living.
Soldiers who come home and show their scars as if they were ornaments. If they can stand that for wages or for a battle, he asks, why can't I stand firm for the good of every being?
Then comes his vow: whatever it costs, he will never bow down to the afflictions. Notice what the warrior does in that verse. He doesn't hate himself.
He doesn't punish the craving or pretend it isn't there. The enemy is still pushing. He just doesn't bow.
That's a body word, and it's worth feeling in the body. A craving arrives like a shove: a lean toward the fridge, the phone, the sharp reply. Standing firm isn't shoving back with all your strength.
It's feet on the ground, knees soft, letting the push arrive and pass while you stay where you are.
Once, and then once more. Warriors in the poem win by not moving.

how: Buddhist teachers often train steadiness with the body first, in the stillness of a seated or standing posture, so that a passing urge can be felt and allowed to fade without being acted on.

games.q: what does “fight like a warrior” mean?
o: joining a group that trains to defend the weak
standing your ground while a craving pushes
attacking a problem with all of your strength

games.q: the warrior's stance — tap the pairs.
p: bear heat and cold for a living
never to bow down to the afflictions

s: Shantideva's warrior fights craving by hating himself for it
he doesn't punish the craving or himself; he simply refuses to bow.
Shantideva points to people who bear hardship for smaller prizes
farmers, fishermen and soldiers put up with much for wages or a battle.
standing firm means the craving stops pushing
the enemy keeps pushing; the warrior just doesn't move.

games.q: you've given up sweets for a month for your health. at a party, someone hands you a brownie. what does a Shantideva-style warrior do first?
o: eat it fast before the guilt has time to arrive.
notice the pull, feel your feet, and let it pass without bowing.
lecture yourself in your head about how weak you are.
games.why: Shantideva's warrior doesn't fight with self-hatred. the push comes; he stands where he is and doesn't bow.

practice: Stand up, if you can, feet hip-width apart, knees a little soft, and feel your weight sink into the floor. If a pull arrives during the sit, an itch, a thought of your phone, notice where it leans in the body.
Let it lean, and keep your feet exactly where they are until it passes.

wordCard.voice: Fight like a warrior: Shantideva's way with craving and anger. Feel the push, don't bow, and stay where you're standing.

orig.note: Sanskrit: enemy. Shantideva pairs it with klesha to speak of the afflictions as enemies.

carryVoice: Your line: stand firm. Feet first, and the rest follows. Four days into chapter four.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 4.40-4.45 (people bear hardship for livelihood; warriors display wounds as ornaments; I will never bow down to the afflictions)
